sentences.text: Jeholosaurus was a small, bipedal herbivore belonging to the neornithischian group of dinosaurs.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — measures 71.1 centimeters in total length, with a tail of 35.6 centimeters, a skull 6.3 centimeters long, and lower jaws each measuring 5.9 centimeters.
Its upper jaw features six teeth in the premaxilla and at least thirteen in the maxilla.
The foot possesses four metatarsals, with the third being the longest at 5.5 centimeters and positioned more toward the front than the others.
Researchers note that Jeholosaurus replaced its maxillary teeth every 46 days, a rate faster than most basal ornithischians.
The first specimens were discovered in 2000 at Lujiatun near Beipiao City in Liaoning Province, China, and described by Xu Xing, Wang Xiaolin, and You Hailu.
The type specimen for the genus is cataloged as IVPP V 12529.

The fossils were preserved in fluvial sandstone and tuff, likely buried by a volcanic eruption that affected a radius of fifty to sixty miles, though other estimates suggest a coverage of 80 to 96 kilometers.
Four additional specimens, including partial and complete skulls, were referred to the species in 2009.

Researchers suggest Jeholosaurus may have been omnivorous because its front teeth resemble carnivores while its back teeth are fan-shaped like herbivores, leading to a debate about whether it ate both plants and animals.
The original describers classified Jeholosaurus only as Ornithischia incertae sedis without assigning it to a specific family.
Later cladistic analyses placed Jeholosaurus in a basal position within the Ornithopoda.
A clade containing Jeholosaurus, Haya, and Changchunsaurus was named Jeholosauridae, and the species is now classified within this family.
However, the Paleobi Database lists the family of Jeholosaurus as Thescelosauridae.

The time range for Jeholosaurus spans from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago, while other sources date the fossils to the Barremian stage approximately 126 to 124 million years ago.
